source: CAMFAD student thesis: "Establishment of a New Coconut Plantation Farm", National School of Agriculture, July 1994
text:
Five diseases of coconut are profiled, mostly affecting nursery seedlings and young palms:

Anthracnose: a fungal disease appearing on young leaves as yellow-brown spots that merge and expand, eventually killing the leaf tissue if untreated and potentially spreading loss across many nursery seedlings. Control: avoid overcrowding seedlings in the nursery bed, ensure good airflow and drainage, remove and destroy infected seedlings promptly, and spray with Captan, Thiram, or Mancozeb (use one); the source cautions against using a copper-based fungicide on young leaves.

Blast: causes round to oval spots on leaves that merge together; seedlings can die within a short time; occurs mainly on plants still bearing juvenile/strap leaves. Control: avoid dense seedling spacing in the nursery, and ensure water does not stand/pool in the nursery bed.

Dry basal rot: causes the base of the plant to dry and rot; leaves yellow and die off progressively from the base upward while the growing tip may initially remain healthy. Control: no effective chemical control is noted; remove and destroy (burn) affected plants.

Vascular wilt: leaves yellow progressively starting with the oldest leaves, then dry from the tip inward (tip dieback), sometimes with premature fruit drop; the disease can spread rapidly between trees. Control: no effective chemical control is noted; monitor for and remove/destroy any tree showing yellowing or wilting symptoms promptly to limit spread.

Basal stem rot: yellowing starts with old leaves and progresses to the crown/bud, with visible rotting or cracking of the trunk near its base and stunted growth. Control: remove and destroy affected trees.

Armillaria root rot: yellowing progresses from old leaves, roots and the root collar rot below ground. Control: remove and destroy (burn) affected trees; this is the consistent recommendation across all the diseases in this list for which no chemical treatment is described as effective — sanitation (prompt removal of diseased plants) is the primary management tool.
